idiom_name: io.circe.Codec with deriveCodec, or a hand-written Encoder/Decoder pair
implementation_notes: circe packages the pattern as a typeclass pair: Codec[A] bundles Encoder[A] (value to Json) and Decoder[A] (Json to value), so one implicit instance owns both directions and neither the case class nor the JSON layer references the other. deriveCodec (semi-automatic) generates both halves once; play-json's Format[T] = Reads[T] + Writes[T] is the equivalent in the Play ecosystem. A hand-written mapper trait with two methods stays justified when the mapping is not serialization, because circe is deliberately Json-specific.
pitfalls: Implicit resolution picks whichever codec is in scope, so explicit instances plus import hygiene beat import io.circe.generic.auto._.
Derivation fails at compile time when one field type lacks an instance, and the implicit search error does not name the field directly.
java.time codecs come from a separate module whose default format may not match the wire contract, so the Instant codec must be declared explicitly.
decodeJson returns Either[Error, A]; discarding the left side turns a boundary failure into an exception far from the seam.

variants.name: scala.jdk.CollectionConverters asScala/asJava (delegating wrappers)
variants.implementation_notes: The standard library's own bidirectional converter: asScala wraps a Java collection as a Scala one and asJava does the reverse, both delegating to the same underlying data instead of copying, and neither collection type knows the other exists. This is the converter-as-adapter shape, right when the two representations are views of the same data; when a copy is wanted the names change to toScala/toJava, which is exactly the distinction a converter has to make explicit.
variants.code_sketch:
import scala.jdk.CollectionConverters.*
import scala.collection.mutable

val javaMap: java.util.Map[String, Int] = new java.util.HashMap()
val scalaView: mutable.Map[String, Int] = javaMap.asScala   // Java -> Scala, no copy
scalaView.put("a", 1)
javaMap.get("a")                                            // 1: the same data
val copied: mutable.Map[String, Int] = javaMap.toScala      // explicit copy
pitfalls: asScala/asJava are views: mutation is visible on both sides, so a caller that expects an independent collection gets aliasing bugs - use toScala/toJava for copies.
A Scala wrapper can offer operations the underlying Java collection does not implement, which fails at call time with UnsupportedOperationException.
Converting inside a hot loop allocates a wrapper per call; hoist the conversion or copy once.
